client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away last year... it's been almost a year now since the accident, and I still can't seem to find any enjoyment in things I used to love. I feel like I've pulled away from my friends too, and honestly it's gotten to the point where I'm not even sure I want to be around people anymore. I guess I'm here because someone told me therapy might help, but I'm not totally convinced it's going to make any difference.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for sharing something so painful — losing your brother, and in such a sudden way, is an enormous loss, and everything you're describing, the withdrawal, the loss of joy, the doubt about whether anything can help, makes a lot of sense given what you've been carrying. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, and I wonder if part of you feels some urgency, or maybe even some anxiety, about being here today despite that uncertainty. It takes real courage to show up even when you're not sure it will work, and I'd love to gently explore together what "making a difference" might even look like for you right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I guess I am speaking fast. I didn't really notice that until you pointed it out, but now that you mention it, there's this kind of tightness in my chest, like I'm bracing for something. I think part of me is scared that if I slow down and actually sit with all of this, it's going to feel even more real than it already does.
therapist: That fear of slowing down makes so much sense — when we've been in survival mode, keeping busy or moving fast can feel like the only thing holding everything together, and stillness can feel genuinely threatening. What you just described, that tightness in your chest, is your body telling you something really important about how much you've been protecting yourself this past year. I'm curious — when you imagine actually slowing down, what is it you're most afraid might surface?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what scares me most is that if I stop moving, I'll have to actually sit with how lonely I've been this past year. Like, as long as I'm busy, I can tell myself I'm fine, I'm productive, I'm handling it — but if I slow down, I'm afraid I'll realize just how disconnected I feel from everyone around me, and I don't know what to do with that. It feels safer to just keep going, even if it's exhausting me.
therapist: What you're describing is such a common and understandable response to grief — keeping busy becomes a kind of armor, but it sounds like that armor is getting really heavy to carry. There's something really honest and brave in what you just named: that underneath all the productivity, there's a deep loneliness that hasn't had space to be acknowledged yet. I'm wondering, when you think about that disconnection from the people around you, is there one person in particular you've been missing — whether that's your brother, or someone still in your life who feels out of reach?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, honestly... it's my brother I keep coming back to. Even though he's gone, I still catch myself wanting to call him when something happens, good or bad, and then that split second of forgetting hits me like a wall all over again. But there's also my friend Carla, who's still very much alive, and I've basically been ghosting her for months because I just don't know how to be around someone who knew him too.
therapist: That moment of reaching for your phone to call him before reality hits — that's one of the most quietly devastating parts of grief, and it makes complete sense that it keeps knocking the wind out of you. What strikes me about Carla is that she might actually be one of the few people who truly understands that loss, and yet that shared connection might also make her feel like a painful reminder rather than a source of comfort right now. I'm curious — when you imagine what it might be like to finally reach out to her, what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think about reaching out to Carla and my stomach just tightens up immediately. Part of me worries that talking to her would just make it more real, like we'd both be sitting there in this awful shared pain with no way out of it. And honestly, I'm also scared she's moved through her grief differently than me, and she'll think I'm still too stuck, or that I'm doing something wrong by not being further along.
therapist: The fear of being judged for where you are in your grief is so painful, especially by someone whose opinion clearly matters to you — and I want to gently offer that grief doesn't have a timeline that you can fall behind on. What you're describing, that worry that Carla might see you as "stuck," sounds like it might also be a reflection of how you've been judging yourself this past year. I'm wondering, if Carla came to you and said she was still struggling this deeply, what would you think of her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because honestly, if Carla came to me and said she was still this torn up over losing someone, I'd just want to hold her and tell her it makes complete sense. I wouldn't think she was weak or pathetic at all. But I guess when it's me, it feels different somehow, like the rules are different for me than they are for everyone else.
therapist: You just discovered something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you'd ever apply to someone you love, and that double standard is quietly making your grief so much harder to bear. That gap between the compassion you'd offer Carla and what you allow yourself is worth sitting with, because somewhere along the way you learned that your pain needs to be earned or justified in a way that other people's doesn't. I'm curious — do you have any sense of where that belief might have come from, that the rules are somehow different for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've been sitting with that question and... honestly, I think it might go back to my mom. She wasn't a bad person, but she always had it harder than everyone else, you know? Like, whatever I was going through, there was always this unspoken message that I shouldn't take up too much space with my feelings because hers were bigger, more real somehow. So yeah, I think I just... absorbed that. That my pain is kind of a lesser version of real pain.
therapist: What you just uncovered is profound — you didn't learn that your pain was unimportant from nowhere, you learned it from someone you loved and needed, and that lesson has been quietly running in the background ever since, including through this entire year of grief. And yet I notice that even as you're saying something so significant, there's a kind of matter-of-fact quality to your voice, like you're describing it from a slight distance — I wonder if part of you is still doing that very thing right now, minimizing how much it actually hurt to grow up feeling like your feelings had to wait. What does it feel like to say out loud, maybe for the first time, that what you absorbed simply wasn't true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... saying it out loud that it wasn't true feels weird, almost like I'm betraying something, like I'm calling my mom a liar or something. And I don't know if I fully believe it yet, because part of me still thinks maybe she was right, maybe I do make too big a deal out of things. It's just... it's sitting kind of heavy right now, more than I expected it to.
therapist: That feeling of betrayal makes so much sense — challenging a belief that came from your mom isn't the same as calling her a liar, it's just recognizing that she was a person with her own wounds who passed something on to you that was never yours to carry. And I want to stay with what you just said at the end, that it's sitting heavier than you expected, because your voice tells me this is landing somewhere really deep right now, even as part of you is trying to hold it together. You don't have to fully believe the new thing yet — that's not how this works — but I'm wondering, what does that heaviness feel like it needs from you in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think... it needs me to just sit with it, maybe, but that's honestly the hardest thing for me to do because I always feel like I have to fix it or push through it or explain it away. There's this part of me that wants to immediately go "okay, so what do I do with this" because just feeling it feels dangerous somehow, like if I let myself really go there I won't be able to come back from it. I don't know if that makes sense, but the heaviness feels like it's asking me to stop running, and I'm not sure I know how to do that.
therapist: It makes complete sense, and what you just described — that fear that feeling it fully means you won't come back — is actually one of the most common things that keeps people running, but I want to offer you something gently: that fear is itself a feeling you've been surviving all year, which means you're already stronger than that belief gives you credit for. You don't have to learn how to sit with everything all at once, and you don't have to do it alone — that's actually part of what this space is for. What if "not running" didn't have to mean diving into the deep end, but just meant pausing here, with me, for one more moment, exactly as you are right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but there's this other part that's like, "she's just saying that because it's her job to say reassuring things." I don't know if I fully trust that I'm as strong as you're making me sound, because from where I'm sitting, I've just been white-knuckling it through the year, not actually coping. But I guess... I'm still here, so maybe that counts for something, even if it doesn't feel like strength.
therapist: I really appreciate you saying that directly to me — that kind of honesty is actually the opposite of what someone who doesn't trust the process would do, and it tells me you're already engaging more genuinely than you might realize. And I want to sit with what you said at the end, because you almost slipped past it: "I'm still here, so maybe that counts for something" — I noticed your voice was moving quite fast again, like you were rushing through the most important thing you've said all session. What would it mean for you to actually let that land, to say "I'm still here" and mean it, without the "even if" that came right after?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
